name: Lena Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a team lead at the member-owned co-op supermarket in our river town. I run the deli counter in the mornings, then swap onto the tills for the lunch rush and cover the floor if someone's off. My favourite part is knowing the regulars: old Mr Aksoy buys the same two slices of ham every Thursday. What wears me out is the lifting and the Saturday queues, plus the fact that I'm also the shop steward, so people bring me their problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've heard this before and it's mostly hype. I'd tell friends to try the tools for small things, like I do for writing the weekly rota note. At work I'd keep it practical: use what helps, ignore what doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine with it, because nothing big moves. Our co-op is cautious and the members like human beings at the counter. But I keep one eye on the self-service tills, they've grown from four to six this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and keep saving, about 120 a month towards our deposit. I'd use the AI tool a bit more, perhaps to plan the deli orders, since it's quicker than the spreadsheet. I'd also keep going to my Tuesday evening union branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled, to be honest. A bit of background worry about rent, but nothing that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're shop steward as well. What would you hear from colleagues in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People would grumble about hours more than about AI. Ruth (a colleague of 30 years) would ask whether the new scanners will make her redundant, and I'd say honestly that I don't think so yet. I'd tell her to ask the manager in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What are the pressures you carry already, AI or no AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent of 580 split with my partner Jonas, a bike mechanic whose work is seasonal, so winter is thin. Our cushion is about three months. That's the pressure that's real, whatever happens with AI.

say: Mostly **hype**: use what helps and ignore what doesn't.
I'd tell friends to try the tools for **small things**, like writing the rota note.
think: Nothing big moves, because our co-op is **cautious** and members want people at the counter.
I still watch the **self-service tills**, which went from four to six.
do: Keep saving about **120 a month** towards a deposit.
Use the AI tool to plan **deli orders** faster than the spreadsheet.
Keep going to my Tuesday **union branch**.
feel: Pretty **settled**, with a background worry about rent.
S0.quote: Our co-op is cautious and the members like human beings at the counter.
fieldNote: Secure in the co-op and calm, though Jonas's **seasonal** pay leaves winters thin.
Already uses AI for small jobs, so the plateau confirms her habits.
Acts as the shop steward and passes questions to management in writing.

steps.text: Save about 120 a month towards a flat deposit
Use an AI tool to plan weekly deli orders
Keep working the deli and tills as usual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's time to talk about training, now, before decisions are made. At work I'd tell the team we should ask the co-op board what's planned. Online I'd share good articles but I wouldn't panic anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering, the rota and the stock counts could all go to software. That's the part of my team-lead job that makes me worth more than a till worker, so it worries me a bit. The shop floor and the deli are safer, because people want a person to cut their cheese.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a short course in using AI properly, and I'd go to the co-op's free evening session on its ordering system. I'd ask the board for a promise that tasks moved to software mean training, not cuts. And I'd look at a part-time nutrition course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, like the first cold week of autumn. Not scary but you notice it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your thinking tasks would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ordering and the weekly forecast would go first, since a program does them in seconds. I'd lose a few hours of desk work on a Wednesday. That's not a lot, but it's the part of my job that shows I'm senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your shop is most exposed in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth, because she doesn't use a computer more than she must, and the young part-timers on the tills. Self-checkouts eat their hours first. I'd sit with Ruth and show her the new ordering screen myself.

say: Time to **talk about training** now, before decisions get made.
I'd ask the co-op **board** what's planned, and share good articles without scaring anyone.
think: Ordering, rota and stock counts could move to **software**, and that is what makes me senior.
The deli and floor feel **safer**, since people want a person.
do: Take a short **AI course** and attend the co-op's evening session.
Ask the board for **training, not cuts**, in writing.
feel: A little **uneasy**, like the first cold week of autumn.
S1.quote: The shop floor and the deli are safer, because people want a person to cut their cheese.
fieldNote: Sees her own **thinking tasks**, ordering and forecasting, as the exposed part of a safe job.
Protective of older colleague Ruth and of part-timers whose hours go first.
Reaches for training and a union ask together.

steps.text: Take a short course on using AI properly
Ask the co-op board for training promises in writing
Look into a part-time nutrition course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government and employers have to sit down with unions right now. I'd ask for a plan, a retraining budget and a pause on laying anyone off. Online I'd be loud, because quiet would let them off the hook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be shaken. Thinking AI by 2028 hits the office jobs, so the money in our town shrinks, and fewer people spend at our shop. Then the robots come around 2031, and the tills and shelves go with them. I'd have maybe three years after 2028 to land somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd sit down with Jonas and do the budget line by line, then cut down to 1,100 a month. I'd sign up for the nutrition course and put the deposit plan on ice. I'd also learn the AI tools properly, because someone has to run the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It'd feel like a clock ticking, though I'd keep telling myself that I'm good at learning new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is not long. What's the first thing you do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that we're okay for now, that we've got three months and a plan, and that I'd rather do something than worry. I'd also say that we should move the wedding talk back a bit, so we'd keep the cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side comes first and it's quick: ordering, scheduling, answering customers. The hands-on side gives me about three more years, which is the window I'd use to retrain. If I wasted that window I'd be angry with myself.

say: Governments and employers must sit down with **unions** right now.
I'd demand a **retraining budget** and a pause on layoffs, loudly and online.
think: Thinking AI shrinks the **office jobs** in town, so fewer people spend at our shop.
Robots in 2031 give me a **three-year window** after 2028.
do: Budget line by line and cut to **1,100 a month**.
Enrol in the **nutrition course** and park the deposit plan.
feel: **Anxious**, like a clock ticking, yet confident that I learn fast.
S2.quote: The hands-on side gives me about three more years, which is the window I'd use to retrain.
fieldNote: Turns fear into a **budget and a course** within the first month.
Reads the gap between thinking AI and robots as a retraining window.
Delays wedding talk to protect her cushion.

steps.text: Cut household spending to 1,100 a month
Press the union and the board for a retraining budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, so let's use it. I'd tell the team to learn something new each year and I'd push the co-op to offer paid study days. Online I'd share what I'm learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's still big, but I'd feel more in control. I'd be 32 by 2031 and the robots around 2034, so my twenties would be spent building a second skill. Probably not the first time I'd change careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd do the nutrition course part-time and keep my deli hours. I'd keep saving 150 a month and I'd try a side bit of work, like helping with the co-op's online orders. I'd use AI at work every week to get properly good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a steady kind. I'd rather have five years of knowing than one year of surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you some room. How would you use it differently from the two-year case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same shape as the quick one, but slower. I'd study in the evenings rather than quit anything, and I wouldn't move the deposit plan. I'd also keep an eye on the local jobs board for care and food-service roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the co-op in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the co-op to guarantee study leave and first call on any new jobs that software creates, like online order management. We're member-owned, so the members could vote for it. I'd stand up at the annual meeting to propose it.

say: We have **time**, so let's use it for learning.
I'd push the co-op for **paid study days** and share what I learn online.
think: I'd be 32 in 2031 and robots arrive around 2034, so my twenties build a **second skill**.
I'd rather have five years of **knowing** than one of surprises.
do: Do the nutrition course **part-time** and keep my deli hours.
Keep saving **150 a month** and try co-op online-order work.
S3.quote: We're member-owned, so the members could vote for it. I'd stand up at the annual meeting to propose it.
fieldNote: More **control** with five years; study comes alongside work, nothing is dropped.
Sees the co-op's member vote as a route for workers' rights.
Keeps deposit plan intact, unlike in the fast scenario.

steps.text: Study nutrition part-time in the evenings
Save 150 a month towards the deposit
Take on co-op online-order work for extra pay
Propose paid study leave at the co-op annual meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years means we can design it properly. I'd be telling people to vote and organise now, since that's when it counts. At work, I'd make sure the younger staff get training time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a decade feels calm to me. I'd be 37 by 2036 and I'd have done my course and had time to think about kids. The robots around 2039 would still touch the tills, but I'd be somewhere else by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the nutrition course and look for a part-time assistant job at the health centre. I'd keep my co-op hours for stability. Jonas and I would buy a place in about four years, and I'd keep using AI for planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit sad about the till days ending, because I do like the regulars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still bother with the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the course, yes. Ten years is long enough to slip into doing nothing, and I'd hate that. A qualification travels, while a till job is tied to one building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good version of this world look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good version is one where the savings from machines pay for people to study and work shorter weeks. I'd have Mr Aksoy still getting his ham from a person, even if the till is a robot. That's the world I'd vote for.

say: Ten years means we can **design** this properly.
I'd tell people to **vote** and organise now, and give younger staff training time.
think: A decade feels **calm**; I'd have the course done and room to think about kids.
The tills may go to robots around **2039**, but I'd be elsewhere.
do: Finish the nutrition course and look for **part-time health-centre work**.
Buy a place with Jonas in about **four years**.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a little sad about the till days ending.
S4.quote: A qualification travels, while a till job is tied to one building.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep the job and add **qualifications** in sequence.
Her picture of a good world is **shared gains**, not nostalgia.
Sadness is about the regulars, not about money.

steps.text: Finish the nutrition course in the next two years
Apply for part-time assistant work at the health centre
Buy a flat with Jonas in about four years
Vote for policies that share machine savings with workers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most, because there's no time to study and save at once. What would help is a retraining budget, study leave from the employer, and an honest conversation with workers before decisions are made. In my own case a union that I'm part of already would be the biggest help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people think shop workers are not paying attention. We watch what's changing every day. If somebody asked us before they bought the machines we'd tell them what works.

headlineQuote: If somebody asked us before they bought the machines we'd tell them what works.
portrait: Lena is a 27-year-old **team lead** at a member-owned co-op in a river town, running the deli and covering tills.
She is the shop **steward**, speaks up for older colleagues like Ruth and trusts unions and co-ops.
She uses AI tools now and then, so she answers change with a course and a budget.
Money is tight but workable: three months saved, rent of 580 and a partner with seasonal pay.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years leaves no time to study and save together.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining budget**, study leave and an honest talk with workers before machines are bought.
